summary: Records the requirements and design considerations behind iSCSI, a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands over TCP/IP so computers can use remote disk and tape devices. It comes from the IP Storage working group's early work.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers talk to hard drives with a set of commands. iSCSI sends those commands over the network, and this document explains what it needed to do and why.

questions: how does scsi run over tcp
subtitle: The goals and trade-offs the IP Storage working group set before designing iSCSI, SCSI storage over TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: Disks and tape libraries were attached to computers by SCSI parallel bus or Fibre Channel, and the IETF wanted to carry that traffic over ordinary IP networks without losing performance, ordering or safety.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out requirements and design considerations for iSCSI: map SCSI onto TCP, work with a single connection but allow several, add digests to catch corruption, and provide authentication, naming and discovery.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that does not define a protocol standard. It records what iSCSI had to achieve and why, so the protocol specification could be judged against it.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: TCP/IP, with SCTP as a possible later substitute

today: RFC 3347 is an Informational document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records requirements and design considerations, not a protocol standard.

sections.title: SCSI Storage over IP
sections.content:
The IP Storage working group was chartered to develop technology to transport block storage data over IP protocols. This includes a protocol to carry the Small Computer Systems Interface (SCSI) over the Internet, called iSCSI. The first version maps SCSI onto TCP/IP so that storage controllers, mainly disk and tape arrays and libraries, can be attached to IP networks such as Gigabit Ethernet and 10 Gigabit Ethernet. The iSCSI protocol is a mapping of SCSI to TCP and is a "SCSI transport" as defined by the ANSI T10 document SCSI SAM-2.

Storage controllers had traditionally been attached by SCSI parallel bus or Fibre Channel. The RFC argues that IP offers competition in the equipment market, a single network type to install and operate, and a rich set of management, security and QoS solutions. It also offers extended distance ranges and connectivity to carrier-class services.

The contemplated applications are local storage access and consolidation, remote access to storage (such as a storage service provider), local and remote mirroring, and backup and recovery. Topologies range from point-to-point links and dedicated storage LANs to shared LANs, LAN-to-WAN links, private networks and the public Internet. The RFC expects sophisticated users to keep storage sub-networks isolated for the best control of security and QoS.

This document describes requirements. It does not define a protocol standard, but it uses the key words of RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a computer's hard drive is plugged in with a special cable. iSCSI lets the computer reach drives through the regular network instead, like getting books from a library across town by delivery rather than walking down the hall.

sections.title: Performance and Cost Goals
sections.content:
iSCSI MUST let implementations equal or improve on the current state of the art for SCSI interconnects, and MUST enable cost-competitive implementations compared with Fibre Channel. It SHOULD minimize control overhead, because storage access is usually stop-and-wait and the interconnect delay, generally around 100 microseconds, directly affects performance.

Host CPU use MUST be equal to or better than current technology. To get there, iSCSI MUST make it possible to build I/O adapters that handle an entire SCSI task, SHOULD permit direct data placement ("zero-copy"), where data goes straight off the wire into its allocated memory with no intermediate copies, and SHOULD NOT impose complex operations on host software.

The protocol MUST provide full use of available link bandwidth and MUST allow an implementation to exploit parallelism with multiple connections. The RFC notes that for competitive speed, the performance path of the full protocol stack will need to be done in hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: The new way of reaching drives must be at least as fast as the old way, cost no more, and not make the computer work harder. Skipping extra copying of data is like carrying a box straight to its shelf instead of setting it down in the hallway first.

sections.title: Framing and Direct Placement
sections.content:
Framing means adding information so an implementation can find the boundaries of an iSCSI protocol data unit (PDU) inside the TCP byte stream. Two needs drive it. The first is an interfacing need: building a message-based protocol on top of a byte stream, which a length field in the header can handle as long as the receiver parses from the start of the stream and never loses alignment. The second is accelerated processing at high data rates, for zero-copy in LANs and for big buffers in high-bandwidth, high-latency WANs.

The RFC gives a worked example: a 10 Gbps pipe with a 200 msec delay holds 250 MB. In a conventional TCP implementation, a lost segment stops stream processing until it is recovered, so the receiver would have to hold that much data in an anonymous buffer and move it later. Some proponents wanted a way to put data directly where it belongs even after a drop.

A length in the header will not serve direct data placement, so the framing mechanism should let the receiver resynchronize PDU boundaries even when a packet is temporarily missing from the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Data on a network arrives as one long ribbon, and the receiver needs to know where each message starts and stops. If a piece of ribbon goes missing, the receiver should still be able to find the next message instead of waiting around.

sections.title: Connections and Command Ordering
sections.content:
SCSI task queuing lets an initiator have several commands outstanding at once, but it only works if commands reach the target in the order the initiator sent them. iSCSI must therefore give ordered transport of SCSI commands, even across different network paths.

iSCSI MUST operate over a single TCP connection to allow lower-cost implementations. For faster devices it should allow multiple connections while behaving as a single SCSI port. The RFC calls this connection binding: the iSCSI layer makes several TCP instances look like one SCSI transport. iSCSI SHOULD support connection binding, and it MUST be optional to implement. The alternative, "wedge" drivers above the SCSI layer, must wait for each request to finish to keep updates ordered.

With several connections, a command and its data and status stay on the same connection (connection allegiance). This is the symmetric approach, where all connections are identical in features. The asymmetric approach, with commands on one connection and data and status on another, was discussed extensively. It gives a simpler protocol on the data connections, but recovery differs depending on which connection fails and it may need more inter-processor communication.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send a stack of numbered letters, they must be read in order. Using several mail routes at once is faster, but the design has to make sure the letters still get read in the right order.

sections.title: Simplicity, Corruption and Recovery
sections.content:
The RFC says that adoption of a protocol is inversely proportional to its complexity. iSCSI SHOULD minimize optional features, MUST negotiate any needed feature at session establishment (login), and MUST work correctly when no optional features are negotiated or when a negotiation fails.

Research papers suggest the TCP checksum lets some bit errors through. So iSCSI MUST support a data integrity check format for generating digests, including a CRC or other digest over the SCSI data block and over each command and status message. Gateways may strip and rebuild iSCSI headers, so a separate header digest is needed. Two header digests, one for the invariant part such as addresses and one for the variant part, are suggested. The header format SHOULD be extensible to other digest methods.

SCSI was designed for a reliable parallel bus, so applications assume transport errors do not happen and recover slowly. iSCSI MUST recover in a timely way from failure of the initiator, the target or the network between them, and MUST specify recovery for non-idempotent requests such as tape drive operations. It SHOULD consider fail-over for mirrored targets, and SHOULD let either side gracefully terminate and restart a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the rules simple, add a check number to every package so damage is noticed, and have a plan for when something breaks, because drives expect the mail never to get lost.

sections.title: Fitting Into IP and SCSI
sections.content:
The specification MUST be clear and unambiguous so independent implementations interoperate. iSCSI MUST be compatible with both IPv4 and IPv6, use TCP connections conservatively, and not require changes to existing Internet protocols. It MUST be designed so SCTP could later replace TCP with minimal changes to operation and PDU formats. It MUST also be a good network citizen with TCP-compatible congestion control as defined in RFC 2914, and MUST NOT use multiple connections to avoid congestion control. Its use of IP addresses and TCP ports MUST be firewall friendly, with connection requests going to a specific well-known port.

On the SCSI side, iSCSI must meet the SCSI Architecture Model (SAM-2) requirements for a transport, and the specification MUST say for each feature whether it is optional, recommended or required. It MUST specify strictly ordered delivery of SCSI commands over a session between an initiator and target, even with transport errors. An implementation that does not need ordering can use multiple sessions per initiator-target pair.

It MUST NOT require changes to SCSI-3 command sets, MUST support all SCSI-3 command sets and device types, SHOULD support ACA (Auto Contingent Allegiance), and MUST allow gateways to other SCSI transports such as parallel SCSI and Fibre Channel FCP. It MUST also handle packet drop, duplication, corruption, stale packets and re-ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system has to get along with the old ones: it must work on today's networks, obey the traffic rules, speak the drives' language unchanged, and be able to talk to older drive systems through a translator.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Directly attached storage had minimal security because the physical connection gave little chance for attack. Carrying block storage over IP opens the door to active attacks, such as identity spoofing and man-in-the-middle, and passive ones, such as eavesdropping.

iSCSI MUST provide strong authentication when more security is needed, and SHOULD need minimal configuration and overhead when running insecurely. It SHOULD allow new security mechanisms without breaking backward compatibility. Authentication MAY range from none to public or private keys. iSCSI MUST support private authenticated login, which means no clear-text passwords at a minimum, and the login MUST resist attacks. It MUST support data origin authentication, which MAY be optional to use, and the requirements should be met with standard protocols such as IPsec or TLS.

iSCSI SHOULD NOT preclude additional integrity protection such as IPsec or TLS, and it MUST provide for a data encryption protocol such as TLS or IPsec ESP for confidentiality between endpoints. The RFC notes that an application may also encrypt blocks before writing them, which gives it the best protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Once drives are reachable over the network, strangers could try to read or fake things. So logging in must be secret and strong, and the data should be lockable in transit.

sections.title: Management, Naming and Discovery
sections.content:
iSCSI SHOULD be manageable with standard IP-based management protocols, but the iSCSI protocol document MUST NOT define a management architecture or explicitly refer to MIBs.

For naming, iSCSI MUST support the SAM-2 naming architecture and MUST identify a storage device with a unique identifier that does not depend on the path used to reach it, so that alternate paths can be correlated. Names MUST come from existing naming authorities and SHOULD be human-readable strings in an international character set. Standard Internet lookup such as DNS SHOULD be used to resolve names. Names must also work with SCSI third-party operations like EXTENDED COPY.

For discovery, iSCSI MUST NOT disturb existing IP discovery techniques and MUST provide some way to tell whether an iSCSI service is available at an IP address, expected to be a well-known port. It MUST provide an optional method to list the SCSI targets available at an end point. Further discovery beyond iSCSI SHOULD use SCSI commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Every drive needs a permanent name that stays the same no matter which road you take to reach it, and a way to ask a server which drives it has.

items.title: Symmetric
items.text: All connections are identical in features. A command, its data and its status stay on one connection (connection allegiance).

items.title: Asymmetric
items.text: Commands go on one connection, data and status on another. Simpler data connections, but recovery differs by connection type.
